lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Say you have a trading idea and you want to know how it behaves on a dozen different instruments, not just the first one you tried. Doing that by hand is tedious. BatchBacktesting turns it into a single repeatable run.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Four steps. Choose your instruments, fetch and clean their prices, run a strategy on each, and save results you can compare. It's an AlgoÉTS repository, written in Python, and it keeps every step visible instead of hiding it behind a dashboard.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So where does the work happen?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: In a runner. For each instrument it picks a price adapter, stock or crypto, cleans the observations, and builds a backtest. The instruments run in parallel through a pool of workers, four by default.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And every run uses the same assumptions?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: That's the point. The defaults are one hundred thousand in starting cash and a commission of two tenths of a percent. Each result is tagged with the instrument and the strategy name, so comparisons stay fair.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: What does a strategy look like?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: The default one is a moving average crossover. It tracks a fast average over twenty periods and a slow one over eighty. When the fast one crosses above the slow one, it closes any position and buys, with a stop ten percent below and a target twenty-five percent above. The mirror image sells short.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: No, the strategy file defines twenty-three, built on indicators like RSI, Bollinger Bands and MACD. Most follow the same pattern, so swapping one for another is easy.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: What do you get at the end?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: A CSV per instrument, an aggregate CSV per strategy, and optionally an HTML chart. There are helpers to rank the instruments, and a published example chart for Apple covering five years, from April 2018 to April 2023.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And if someone is new to all this?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: There's a set of beginner notebooks called Workshop1 that leads right into this runner. The written page has the flow diagram and the details of the crossover maths.
